templates.name: Specify or identify a single fact
Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Present or describe to an already familiar audience

items.subtype: Explain a cause (why a method misleads)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• While alive, organisms take in carbon-14, a radioactive isotope of carbon, at roughly the level found in the atmosphere.
• After death, this carbon-14 decays at a predictable rate, so radiocarbon dating treats lower levels as evidence of greater age.
• Limestone formed millions of years ago, and its original carbon-14 has entirely decayed.
• Rivers flowing across limestone gradually dissolve parts of the rock, adding its ancient carbon to the water.
• Freshwater mussels construct their shells from carbon dissolved in the surrounding water.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why radiocarbon dating can overestimate the age of mussel shells from rivers that flow across limestone. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: After a mussel dies, the carbon-14 in its shell decays at a predictable rate, which is why older shells contain less carbon-14 than younger ones do.
Mussels in rivers that flow across limestone build their shells partly from the rock’s carbon, which has no carbon-14 left, so the shells seem older than they are.
Because limestone adds carbon-14 to rivers flowing across it, mussels living there build shells with more carbon-14 than the atmosphere holds, so the shells seem older.
Rivers flowing across limestone dissolve parts of the rock, adding carbon that formed millions of years ago to the water that mussels live in.
items.explanation: Radiocarbon dating reads low carbon-14 as a sign of age. Mussels in limestone rivers build their shells partly from the rock’s carbon, which has lost all its carbon-14, so the shells start out low in carbon-14. Choice B makes that link and so explains why the shells seem older than they are.

A.recipe: PART (how the method works, not why it errs)
A.why_wrong: It explains how radiocarbon dating works in general but says nothing about limestone or why these shells seem too old.

C.why_wrong: The notes say limestone’s carbon-14 has entirely decayed, so the rock adds carbon with no carbon-14, not extra carbon-14; more carbon-14 would also make a shell seem younger, not older.

D.why_wrong: It gives the first step, ancient carbon entering the water, but never connects it to the shells or their carbon-14, so it does not explain the dating error.

items.notes: Subject: science (radiocarbon dating, the hard-water effect). No named people. Band 6 as planned: one goal-shaped FALSE (C, reversed cause), two PART (A the method alone, D the cause without its link to the shells). Key B draws on bullets 2 to 5 and states a derived link (the shells start low in carbon-14) that no bullet states.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations

band7.why: band_target 6. EXPL on d4b07ce6’s band-6 shape (PART, FALSE, PART): the key links four bullets into a claim no bullet states (the shells start low in carbon-14); C is goal-shaped but reverses the cause and contradicts itself (more carbon-14 would make a shell seem younger), so it falls fast. A strong band 6.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Waru waru are raised planting beds separated by water-filled canals, built on the high plains around Lake Titicaca.
• Andean farmers began building waru waru more than two millennia ago.
• The canals absorb solar heat during the day and release it overnight, protecting crops from frost.
• Farmers later abandoned the fields, which then remained unused for centuries.
• In the 1980s, researchers and local farmers rebuilt several fields, whose potato harvests surpassed those of neighboring fields.
items.stem: The student wants to summarize the history of waru waru. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: For more than two millennia, waru waru have protected crops from frost around Lake Titicaca, and in the 1980s their potato harvests surpassed those of neighboring fields.
Waru waru protect crops from frost because their canals absorb solar heat during the day and release it overnight.
First built by researchers and local farmers in the 1980s, waru waru now protect potato crops from frost on the high plains around Lake Titicaca.
Andean farmers built waru waru more than two millennia ago and later abandoned them, but fields rebuilt in the 1980s outproduced neighboring fields.
items.explanation: The notes give three stages: farmers built waru waru more than two millennia ago, later abandoned them for centuries, and in the 1980s rebuilt some fields that outproduced neighboring ones. Choice D covers all three in order.

A.why_wrong: It presents waru waru as protecting crops for more than two millennia without a break, but the notes say the fields remained unused for centuries before the 1980s.

B.why_wrong: It explains how the canals protect crops from frost, not the history of waru waru.

C.why_wrong: Researchers and farmers rebuilt waru waru in the 1980s; Andean farmers first built them more than two millennia earlier.

items.notes: Subject: history and agriculture (Andean raised fields). No named people; facts kept general (more than two millennia; 1980s revival). Option check: A FALSE and goal-shaped (spans the arc, erases the gap), C FALSE and goal-shaped (wrong builders and date), B true but off-goal (mechanism). Goal-only solve (no notes): A, C and D all read as histories. Derived relation: “outproduced” compresses bullet 5.
band7_moves: band-6 overview shape (key spans origin, decline and revival in one sentence)
two goal-shaped FALSE options that also read as histories: one erases the centuries of abandonment, one moves the origin to the 1980s
one accurate off-goal option built from the mechanism bullet

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations; ancient origin, centuries of disuse and 1980s revival read as accurate

band7.why: 964c6055’s shape plus the section 5 OVERVIEW recipe: two goal-shaped FALSE options and one OG. A carries it: it spans two millennia to the 1980s like the key and fails only once the student sees that “for more than two millennia ... have protected” implies unbroken use, which bullet 4 (centuries unused) contradicts. C dies to one obvious fact (bullet 2) and B is plainly off goal. Goal fit leaves A, C and D; notes well above the rare-word floor. No bullet restates the history, so no second overview passes.

items.subtype: Generalization one level up (the kind of records)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Since 1443, priests at a Shinto shrine beside Japan’s Lake Suwa have documented when the lake freezes each winter.
• These observations are recorded as part of a religious ceremony.
• Since 1354, officials in Beaune, France, have documented the date on which they permitted each year’s grape harvest to begin.
• Freezing is delayed by mild winters, and grapes ripen earlier after hot summers.
• Climatologists have used both records to reconstruct temperatures from centuries before thermometers were widespread.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about the kinds of records that can help climatologists reconstruct past temperatures. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Records kept for nonscientific purposes, from religious ceremonies to grape harvests, can help climatologists reconstruct past temperatures.
Since 1354, officials in Beaune have documented the date on which they permitted each year’s grape harvest to begin.
Climatologists reconstruct past temperatures mainly from records that priests and town officials kept in order to monitor the weather.
Lake Suwa’s freezing records, documented since 1443, are older than Beaune’s harvest records, which began in 1354.
items.explanation: Neither record was made for science: one belongs to a religious ceremony and the other notes when officials allowed each grape harvest to begin, yet climatologists have used both to reconstruct past temperatures. Choice A states that general point about the kind of records involved.

B.why_wrong: It describes one of the two records; it makes no generalization about the kinds of records.

C.why_wrong: The notes say the Lake Suwa record belongs to a religious ceremony and the Beaune record notes when officials permitted the harvest to begin; neither was kept to monitor the weather, and nothing says climatologists rely mainly on such records.

D.why_wrong: Beaune’s records began in 1354, nearly a century before Lake Suwa’s began in 1443, so the Lake Suwa records are the younger set; the comparison is also not a generalization.

items.notes: Subject: science and history (climate records). No named people; both record series are real and well known in climate science. Option check: B true but specific, C FALSE and goal-shaped (a generalization with the wrong purpose), D FALSE (reversed dates). Goal-only solve: A and C both make a generalization about the records. Derived relation: “nonscientific purposes” is stated by no bullet.
band7_moves: the generalization climbs a level, from two named records to the kind of record (2c61e0b9 style)
a goal-shaped FALSE generalization about the same class that misstates why the records were kept
a FALSE comparison that needs the two start dates checked

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Lake Suwa freeze records (from 1443) and Beaune harvest dates (from 1354) read as accurate; climatologists unnamed, no invented finding

band7.why: Like 2c61e0b9 and 3b02e88a the key climbs a level (“records kept for nonscientific purposes”, stated by no bullet) against true specifics, and C adds a goal-shaped FALSE generalization (weather-monitoring purpose, “mainly”). D dies to one date check. Goal fit leaves A and C; no bullet states the generalization.

items.subtype: Relative degree on two measures that point opposite ways
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The wandering albatross is a seabird that spends most of its life gliding above the Southern Ocean.
• Its wingspan can reach 3.5 meters, and adults weigh up to approximately 12 kilograms.
• The Andean condor is a vulture that lives in the mountains of western South America.
• Its wingspan can reach 3.3 meters, and adults weigh up to approximately 15 kilograms.
• Both species depend on prevailing winds and rising air to stay aloft with little flapping.
items.stem: The student wants to compare the size of the wandering albatross with that of the Andean condor. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: With wingspans of up to 3.5 and 3.3 meters, respectively, the Andean condor and the wandering albatross are both remarkably large soaring birds.
The wandering albatross is larger than the Andean condor by both measures, with a wingspan of up to 3.5 meters and a weight of up to approximately 15 kilograms.
The wandering albatross can have a slightly wider wingspan than the Andean condor, but the condor can weigh about 3 kilograms more.
Both the wandering albatross and the Andean condor depend on prevailing winds and rising air to stay aloft with little flapping.
items.explanation: Each bird is larger by a different measure: the albatross’s wingspan can reach 3.5 meters against the condor’s 3.3, but the condor can weigh up to about 15 kilograms against the albatross’s 12. Choice C compares the two on both measures and states each difference correctly.

A.why_wrong: “Respectively” gives the condor the 3.5-meter wingspan and the albatross the 3.3-meter one, the reverse of the notes; it also only calls both birds large rather than comparing them.

B.why_wrong: The albatross has the wider wingspan, but the notes give the condor, not the albatross, a weight of up to approximately 15 kilograms; the albatross weighs up to about 12, so it is not larger by both measures.

D.recipe: OG (a similarity in how they fly)
D.why_wrong: It states how both birds stay aloft; it does not compare their sizes.

items.notes: Subject: science (two large soaring birds); maximum sizes are textbook figures, rounded. No named people. Option check: A FALSE (swapped wingspans), B FALSE and goal-shaped (overall comparison with the condor’s weight given to the albatross), D true but off-goal. Goal-only solve: B and C both compare the birds on both measures. The key’s derived claims (“slightly wider”, “about 3 kilograms more”) appear in no bullet and are comfortably true.
band7_moves: two measures that point opposite ways (wingspan favors the albatross, weight the condor), as in 5fa51c86
key states both relations with derived amounts instead of the raw numbers
goal-shaped FALSE option with a ratio that only arithmetic rules out
a misattached-number option built with “respectively”, plus one off-goal similarity

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people; textbook maximum sizes, rounded
fixes: B rewritten: it mirrored the key (albatross wider, but condor “nearly twice” as heavy) and fell to one ratio check; now a goal-shaped FALSE overall comparison that gives the albatross the condor’s 15 kilograms; B recipe, why_wrong and notes updated

band7.why: Section 5 RANK shape: two measures pointing opposite ways, a key with derived relations (“slightly wider”, “about 3 kilograms more”). Both FALSE options fall to one bullet check each (A’s “respectively” swaps the wingspans; B gives the albatross the condor’s 15 kilograms), but neither shows from goal fit, and 5fa51c86’s own distractors are true LIST options, so this is no weaker than the official band-7 RANK. As drafted, B mirrored the key with one wrong ratio, a pilot tell; rewritten.

items.subtype: Begin a narrative at the chronological start
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Living in Bondage (1992) is a Nigerian drama filmed in the Igbo language.
• Its producer, Kenneth Nnebue, was an electronics merchant with a substantial inventory of blank videocassettes.
• Hoping to make the tapes more marketable, he decided to record a film on them.
• Distributed directly on videocassette, the film sold hundreds of thousands of copies.
• It is widely credited with launching Nollywood, Nigeria’s now enormous filmmaking industry.
items.stem: The student wants to begin a narrative about the making of Living in Bondage. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Distributed directly on videocassette, Living in Bondage sold hundreds of thousands of copies and is credited with launching Nollywood, Nigeria’s film industry.
After Nollywood films had made videocassettes popular across Nigeria, electronics merchant Kenneth Nnebue decided to record a film of his own.
Looking for a way to sell his blank videocassettes, electronics merchant Kenneth Nnebue decided to record a film on them: Living in Bondage.
Kenneth Nnebue’s 1992 Igbo-language drama would go on to sell hundreds of thousands of copies on videocassette.
items.explanation: A narrative about how the film was made should start where the story starts: a merchant with blank tapes he hoped to sell decides to record a film on them. Choice C begins there and names both Nnebue and Living in Bondage.

A.why_wrong: It summarizes the film’s sales and legacy, the end of the story, so it does not begin a narrative about how the film was made.

B.why_wrong: It opens like a story, but the notes credit Living in Bondage with launching Nollywood; Nollywood films did not come first.

D.recipe: PART (jumps ahead; the film goes unnamed)
D.why_wrong: It skips to the film’s later sales without naming it or telling how it came to be made.

items.notes: Subject: arts (film history, Nigeria). Real people and film; the blank-tapes origin is the widely reported account of how the film came about. Cross-skill check: an official Form, Structure, and Sense item mentions Nollywood (Iké Udé’s Nollywood Portraits); this item’s subject is a different work, and the goal names the film, not the industry. Option check: B FALSE and goal-shaped (a narrative opening with the cause reversed), A off-goal (outcome), D partial. Goal-only solve: B and C both open a story.
band7_moves: band-6 narrative shape (key starts at the chronological beginning and names the person and the work, as af88c47a A does)
added a goal-shaped FALSE opening that reverses cause and effect (Nollywood before the film)
one outcome-first option and one jump-ahead option that leaves the film unnamed

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Kenneth Nnebue and Living in Bondage (1992) carry only the widely reported blank-tapes account, no invented finding

band7.why: af88c47a’s shape (OG outcome, PART that jumps ahead with “would go on to”) plus the section 5 goal-shaped FALSE: B opens a story like the key but reverses the cause, which only bullet 5 (the film launched Nollywood) exposes. Goal fit leaves B and C. The key paraphrases the motive (“looking for a way to sell”) and begins at the chronological start, as NARR keys do.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Wind sculpts desert sand into dunes, whose forms depend on the prevailing wind patterns.
• Barchan dunes develop where the wind blows predominantly from a single direction.
• They are crescent shaped, with two horns extending downwind.
• Star dunes develop where the wind direction shifts frequently.
• They have three or more arms radiating from a central summit, which can rise hundreds of meters.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how the shape of a star dune differs from that of a barchan dune. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Unlike a barchan dune, which forms a crescent with two horns, a star dune has three or more arms radiating from a central summit.
Both barchan dunes and star dunes take their forms from the prevailing wind patterns in the places where they develop.
Barchan dunes develop where the wind blows predominantly from one direction, whereas star dunes develop where its direction shifts frequently.
A star dune has three or more arms radiating from a central summit, which can rise hundreds of meters.
items.explanation: The goal names shape. Choice A sets the barchan dune’s crescent beside the star dune’s three or more arms around a central summit.

B.why_wrong: It states something the two kinds of dunes have in common, not a difference in shape.

C.why_wrong: It contrasts the wind conditions in which the dunes develop, not their shapes.

D.why_wrong: It describes only the star dune’s shape and never mentions the barchan dune.

items.notes: Subject: science (desert dunes). General knowledge; no named people. Distractor mix REL, REL, PART (b1’s DIFF items used REL, VAGUE, PART).

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Fresco is a technique for painting murals on plaster walls.
• In buon fresco, pigments mixed with water are applied to still-damp plaster.
• As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction binds the pigments permanently into the wall.
• In fresco secco, pigments mixed with a binder such as egg are painted onto dry plaster.
• Because this paint remains on the surface, it is considerably more vulnerable to flaking.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast how well the two kinds of fresco hold up over time. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Buon fresco is painted on still-damp plaster, whereas fresco secco is painted on plaster that has already dried.
Fresco, a technique for painting murals on plaster walls, can be done on either damp or dry plaster.
Because buon fresco and fresco secco are made in different ways, the two kinds of fresco do not hold up equally well over time.
Buon fresco’s pigments become bound into the wall itself, while fresco secco’s paint remains on the surface and flakes more easily.
items.explanation: To contrast how the two hold up, the sentence must say which lasts better and why. Choice D does: buon fresco’s pigments are bound into the wall, while fresco secco’s paint remains on the surface and flakes more easily.

A.why_wrong: It contrasts the plaster each kind is painted on, not how well each holds up over time.

B.why_wrong: It defines fresco and notes the two methods without saying anything about how they last.

C.why_wrong: It says the two do not hold up equally well but never says which lasts longer or why.

items.notes: Subject: arts (mural technique). General knowledge; no named people. Distractor mix REL, OG, VAGUE.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations

items.subtype: Describe a design to an unfamiliar audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A woonerf, Dutch for “living yard,” is a residential street shared by pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists.
• The design originated in the Netherlands during the 1970s.
• A woonerf has no curbs, so the roadway and sidewalk form one continuous surface.
• Trees, benches, and planters are positioned in the roadway to slow vehicles.
• Variations of the design now appear in cities across Europe and North America.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the layout of a woonerf to an audience unfamiliar with the concept. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A woonerf has no curbs, and trees, benches, and planters are positioned in the roadway to slow vehicles.
A woonerf, a Dutch residential street shared by pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists, has no curbs and places trees and benches in the roadway.
Originating in the Netherlands during the 1970s, the woonerf, a street shared by pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists, has since spread to cities across Europe and North America.
The woonerf, a street design from the Netherlands, is laid out quite differently from an ordinary residential street.
items.explanation: An unfamiliar audience first needs to know what a woonerf is. Choice B identifies it as a Dutch residential street shared by pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists and then describes its layout: no curbs, with trees and benches in the roadway.

A.why_wrong: It describes the layout but never says what a woonerf is, which an unfamiliar audience would need.

C.why_wrong: It identifies the woonerf but tells where it began and spread, not how it is laid out.

D.why_wrong: It says the layout is unusual without describing it.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban design). General knowledge; no named people. Distractor mix AUD, OG, VAGUE.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations

items.subtype: Present an outcome to an audience unfamiliar with a legal concept
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Terra nullius, Latin for “land belonging to no one,” was a legal doctrine treating Australia as unowned before British colonization.
• In 1982, Eddie Koiki Mabo, a Meriam man from the Torres Strait Islands, sued for recognition of his people’s ownership of their traditional lands.
• In 1992, months after Mabo’s death, Australia’s High Court ruled for the Meriam plaintiffs, rejecting terra nullius.
• The ruling led to the Native Title Act of 1993, which established a process for Indigenous land claims.
items.stem: The student wants to present the outcome of Mabo’s case to an audience unfamiliar with terra nullius. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In 1992, Australia’s High Court sided with the Meriam plaintiffs, rejecting terra nullius, the doctrine that Australia had no owners before British colonization.
In 1992, months after Mabo’s death, Australia’s High Court ruled for the Meriam plaintiffs and rejected terra nullius.
In 1982, Eddie Koiki Mabo, a Meriam man from the Torres Strait Islands, filed a lawsuit seeking recognition of his people’s ownership of their traditional lands.
Terra nullius, Latin for “land belonging to no one,” was a legal doctrine treating Australia as unowned before British colonization.
items.explanation: The outcome is the High Court’s 1992 ruling for the Meriam plaintiffs, which rejected terra nullius. Because the audience does not know that term, Choice A also says what it was: the doctrine that Australia had no owners before British colonization.

B.why_wrong: It gives the outcome but uses “terra nullius” without explaining it to an audience that does not know the term.

C.why_wrong: It describes how the case began in 1982, not how it ended.

D.why_wrong: It explains terra nullius but says nothing about the ruling in Mabo’s case.

items.notes: Subject: history and law (Australian land rights). Real case and people, well-known facts (1982 suit, Mabo’s death early in 1992, the 1992 ruling, the Native Title Act of 1993); no web check (WAVE.md). Distractor mix AUD, OG, PART.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Mabo case (1982 suit, his death early in 1992, the 1992 ruling, Native Title Act 1993) reads as accurate; real people carry no invented finding

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Parícutin is a cinder cone volcano in the Mexican state of Michoacán.
• It emerged in February 1943, when smoke and ash began rising from a fissure in a farmer’s cornfield.
• Within a year, its cone had grown more than 330 meters tall.
• Over subsequent years, its lava buried two neighboring towns, leaving only a church tower standing.
• The eruption finally ended in 1952.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how quickly Parícutin grew. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Parícutin erupted for nine years, from its emergence in a farmer’s cornfield in 1943 until 1952.
Over subsequent years, lava from Parícutin buried two neighboring towns, leaving only a church tower standing.
Within just a year of emerging from a cornfield in 1943, Parícutin had grown more than 330 meters tall.
Parícutin, a volcano in Michoacán, Mexico, emerged from a fissure in a farmer’s cornfield in February 1943.
items.explanation: Speed is a height reached in a short time. Choice C stresses that within just a year of emerging, Parícutin had grown more than 330 meters tall.

A.why_wrong: It stresses how long the eruption lasted, not how fast the volcano grew.

B.why_wrong: It describes the damage the lava caused, not the volcano’s growth.

D.why_wrong: It tells where and when the volcano appeared but says nothing about how it grew.

items.notes: Subject: science (volcanology). Well-known facts about a real volcano; no named people. Distractor mix OG, OG, OG, with A a duration trap.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Parícutin (1943 cornfield fissure, over 330 m in a year, two towns buried, ended 1952) reads as accurate

items.subtype: Emphasize an extent (how much was lost)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1403, China’s Yongle Emperor ordered scholars to gather the knowledge of the time into a single encyclopedia.
• More than 2,000 scholars contributed to the project.
• Completed in 1408, the Yongle Encyclopedia filled 11,095 volumes.
• Over the following centuries, most volumes were destroyed or lost through fire, war, and looting.
• Fewer than 400 volumes survive today, held in libraries around the world.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how much of the Yongle Encyclopedia has been lost. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: More than 2,000 scholars contributed to the Yongle Encyclopedia, which filled 11,095 volumes.
Of the Yongle Encyclopedia’s 11,095 volumes, fewer than 400 survive today.
Over the centuries, volumes of the Yongle Encyclopedia were destroyed or lost through fire, war, and looting.
Commissioned in 1403, the Yongle Encyclopedia was completed five years later, in 1408.
items.explanation: Setting the two numbers side by side shows the scale of the loss: fewer than 400 of 11,095 volumes remain. Choice B does that.

A.why_wrong: It emphasizes how large the encyclopedia was, not how much of it has been lost.

C.why_wrong: It says volumes were lost and how, but not how many, so it does not show how much is gone.

D.why_wrong: It gives how long the encyclopedia took to complete.

items.notes: Subject: history (Ming dynasty). Well-known figures (11,095 volumes; fewer than 400 survive), rounded; no web check. Key needs two bullets (total and survivors), as 1.16 does.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Yongle Encyclopedia (1403 to 1408, 2,000-plus scholars, 11,095 volumes, fewer than 400 surviving) reads as accurate

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• American Sign Language (ASL) is largely unrelated to British Sign Language, even though English predominates in both countries.
• In 1817, the first permanent school for deaf students in the United States opened in Hartford, Connecticut.
• One of its cofounders, Laurent Clerc, was a deaf educator from France.
• Clerc taught in French Sign Language, which gradually blended with signs his students already used.
• Today, ASL shares numerous signs with French Sign Language.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why ASL shares numerous signs with French Sign Language. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Even though English predominates in both the United States and Britain, ASL is largely unrelated to British Sign Language.
In 1817, Laurent Clerc, a deaf educator from France, helped found the first permanent school for deaf students in the United States, in Hartford, Connecticut.
The numerous signs that ASL shares with French Sign Language reflect the long history of deaf education in the United States.
ASL shares numerous signs with French Sign Language because Laurent Clerc, a deaf educator from France, used it to teach at the first permanent US school for deaf students.
items.explanation: The notes link the shared signs to Laurent Clerc, a deaf educator from France who taught in French Sign Language at the first permanent US school for deaf students. Choice D states that cause and connects it to the shared signs with “because.”

A.why_wrong: It contrasts ASL with British Sign Language and does not explain the link to French Sign Language.

B.why_wrong: It says who Clerc was and what he helped found but never says he taught in French Sign Language or connects that to ASL.

C.why_wrong: It gestures at history without saying what happened, so it does not explain why the languages share signs.

items.notes: Subject: social science (sign language history). Real people and school, well-known facts; no web check. Distractor mix OG, PART, VAGUE.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Laurent Clerc and the 1817 Hartford school read as accurate; no invented finding
fixes: key D: “the first US school” now “the first permanent US school”, matching bullet 2

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The balafon is a wooden xylophone from West Africa.
• Musicians strike its wooden keys with mallets, and gourds suspended beneath the keys amplify the sound.
• The berimbau is a single-stringed musical bow from Brazil, traditionally played to accompany capoeira, a martial art.
• Musicians tap its steel string with a stick, and a gourd fastened to the bow amplifies the sound.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the balafon and the berimbau. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both the balafon and the berimbau use gourds to amplify their sound.
The balafon has numerous wooden keys, whereas the berimbau has a single steel string.
Traditionally played to accompany capoeira, a martial art, the berimbau is a musical bow from Brazil.
Gourds suspended beneath the balafon’s wooden keys amplify the instrument’s sound.
